title: Tenant sidecar routing & control plane handoffs
content:
Context and purpose:

This is a working note exploring a sidecar-driven approach to tenant routing and control-plane handoffs across the three serving modes: Hosted, Dedicated, Private. Goal is to surface a concrete set of responsibilities, isolation boundaries, and failure-mode behaviors that are:
- consistent for SDK customers,
- operable across multi-region/topology (primary/secondary) setups, and
- friendly to enterprise/private deployments that require clear egress and control-plane separation.

Why a sidecar?
- Many teams have asked for a minimal, deployable artifact that can encapsulate per-tenant routing decisions without forcing changes to the global gateway.
- Sidecars enable localized egress policies, tenant-specific TLS and KMS integrations, and clearer boundaries for private deployments.
- They are a pragmatic bridge between fully centralized control-plane routing and fully client-driven routing policies.

High-level model (one-paragraph):
Each tenant may be associated with a lightweight routing sidecar running in the same tenant compute boundary (hosted node, dedicated pool node, or customer VPC). The global control plane maintains policy and global state (model catalog, region preferences, fallbacks) and publishes signed routing blobs to sidecars. At request time the SDK/gateway consults the local sidecar for the preferred endpoint and routing metadata. Sidecar performs local health checks and fast fallback (e.g., route to a regional compatible variant) without round-tripping to the control plane for every request.

Responsibilities by surface (short bullets)
- Global control plane:
  - Model catalog, compatibility matrix (quantization/variant mapping), global quotas, and SLA tiers.
  - Policy distribution (signed manifests) and rollout orchestration (canary flags, kill-switch).
  - Identity issuance (short-lived control tokens) and cross-region routing rules.
- Sidecar:
  - Enforce tenant-level egress and networking policy (egress endpoints, NAT, proxy config).
  - Localized affinity: sticky routing to dedicated pools when commitments exist.
  - Health aggregation: quick circuit-breaker decisions and local fallback to pre-approved variants.
  - Cache signed manifests and metrics; expose observability hooks (trace ids, per-route latency).
- Gateway/Edge:
  - Fast path TLS termination, global rate limiting, and DDoS protection.
  - Route to sidecar when available; otherwise consult control plane.

Differences across modes (focused comparison)
- Hosted (Redwood-managed compute + control plane):
  - Isolation: logical tenancy enforced by sidecar + per-tenant pool mapping. Sidecar runs in a shared node but scoped to tenant via cgroups/namespaces.
  - Control plane trust: high; sidecar receives signed manifests from Redwood control plane.
  - Egress: outbound to customer endpoints not allowed unless approved; default egress is Redwood internal model endpoints.
  - Failure behavior: sidecar fallbacks to region-compatible hosted variant; global control plane fallback policy active.

- Dedicated (customer-dedicated GPU pools in Redwood infra):
  - Isolation: stronger per-tenant affinity — sidecar pinned to tenant's reserved pools.
  - Control plane trust: medium; manifests flow over private links, optional mTLS.
  - Egress: limited customer-configurable egress for webhooks/logging. Sidecar enforces egress ACLs.
  - Failure behavior: sidecar prefers local dedicated pools. If local capacity exhausted, sidecar consults control plane for permitted spillover targets (could be other dedicated pools or hosted compatible variants depending on contract).

- Private (customer VPC / on-prem):
  - Isolation: physical tenancy; sidecar runs in customer network and acts as the canonical router.
  - Control plane trust: low by default; only policy artifacts signed and verifiable. Optionally air-gapped sync via file manifests.
  - Egress: fully customer-controlled. Sidecar must integrate with customer KMS/HSM and audit.
  - Failure behavior: offline-first. Sidecar uses locally-cached models/variants and only attempts control-plane fetches when network allows. Graceful degradation to smaller quantized variants is preferred over routing outside customer network.

Control-plane to sidecar communication model
- Signed manifests (JSON Web Signatures) published to an object store (or S3-compatible for private) with versioning.
- Sidecar periodically polls or is pushed updates via a dedicated channel (gRPC stream) depending on deployment.
- Manifest contents: model_id -> allowed_endpoints, fallback_chain (ordered list), quantization_hint, latency_slo, allowed_egress_prefixes, allowed_side_effect_domains (for webhooks), rollout_flags.

Latency and SLO implications
- Fast path requires sidecar decisions local to gateway/SDK within 2ms added latency. Keep manifests compact; precompute endpoint resolution tables for common prefixes.
- Control-plane fallbacks (when sidecar requests new manifest or requests spillover permission) are expected to be higher latency; mark these operations as background or rate-limited.

Multi-region behavior and affinity policies
- Preferred-region policy: manifests include ordered region preference; sidecar keeps in-memory affinity counters.
- Burst spillover policy: threshold-based. If throughput exceeds X tokens/s for tenant for >Y seconds and local pools saturated, sidecar consults control plane for spillover. Control plane returns signed permit with TTL.
- Geo-sovereignty: for Private tenants with sovereignty constraints, sidecar refuses to route outside allowed region list regardless of permit.

Failure modes and recommended handling (operational playbook)
- Sidecar-day-0-broken (failed to start): Gateway falls back to control plane edge routing; tenant experiences no local affinity. Pager: platform on-call.
- Manifest verification failure: reject the manifest; sidecar continues using last-known-good. Emit alert if TTL expired.
- Capacity spillover denied: sidecar soft-queues requests and sends backpressure error to SDK with clear retry-after and fallback information. Metrics: per-tenant drop rate and backpressure latency.
- Control plane outage (global): sidecar runs in autonomy mode using cached manifests. For hosted mode we allow best-effort routing to hosted-compatible variants; for private mode we refuse cross-network routing.

Observability hooks (what sidecar must emit)
- per-request resolution id, resolved_endpoint, manifest_version, fallback_reason, egress_decision, trace_id.
- counters: endpoint_503s, local_circuit_trips, spillover_permits_used, manifest_pull_latency.
- sample traces for any request that triggers cross-mode fallback.

Security considerations
- All manifests signed by control plane root keys; sidecar enforces key rotation checks.
- Sidecar must not accept unsigned or unauthenticated spillover permits.
- For private mode, sidecar has pluggable KMS adapter (HSM/KMS) to sign/verify internal logs if required.

Rollout strategy (minimal safe path)
1) Prototype: implement read-only sidecar that only exposes read APIs and uses existing gateway for routing. Canary with a single non-critical tenant.
2) Add manifest verification and local fallback behavior. Run in hosted first (we control infra).
3) Dedicated: enable affinity pins and spillover permit flow. Run a small set of dedicated customers who have agreed to extended telemetry.
4) Private: ship file-sync and air-gap manifest option and test with one SOC/regulated customer.

Open questions / TODOs
- How large can manifests grow before sidecar memory/CPU costs become material? (Diego to run simulated tenant-count tests)
- TTL/refresh policy: poll vs push trade-offs for scale. (Ava to prototype gRPC streaming)
- Standardizing spillover permit format across hosted/dedicated/private. (spec draft needed)
- SDK contract: what error codes do we return when sidecar enforces backpressure vs when control plane denies spillover? (Design to match product SLOs)

Relevant links and references (working):
- JIRA-PLAT-2107: sidecar manifest format
- github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/489: initial sidecar prototype
- slack: #platform-routing thread: "sidecar-approach"

Notes to reviewers:
- This note is intentionally prescriptive but pragmatic; I want feedback specifically around:
  1) whether sidecar responsibilities are too broad (should we keep it narrower?),
  2) how to guarantee low-latency decisioning without overloading sidecar memory, and
  3) whether our proposed failure semantics for Private mode are acceptable for SOC customers.

Quick TODOs (short):
- [ ] Diego: run manifest-size perf test by 2026-01-05
- [ ] Ava: prototype streaming update path by 2026-01-22
- [ ] Liam: draft permit token spec by 2026-02-02

----
End of working note.
